summary: The article provides a generally reliable overview of small-cap stock corrections in India, with most factual claims aligning with authoritative sources. The core assertion about narrowed corrections post-COVID is attributed to a specific expert and supported by a news report.

claims.claim: Small-cap stock corrections in India have become notably less severe post-COVID, averaging around 25% compared to earlier, deeper downturns.
claims.note: Samir Vartak of SageOne Investment Managers is quoted in Livemint stating that post-COVID, the average decline has been closer to 25%, compared to 40-45% in the pre-COVID period.

claims.claim: The recent observation by Samir Vartak of SageOne Investment Managers suggests that this pattern has changed post-COVID. Now, even during market pullbacks, small-cap stocks tend to correct by a more moderate 25%.
claims.note: Samir Vartak, founder and chief investment officer of SageOne Investment Managers, is quoted in Mint stating this.

claims.claim: Small-cap companies, as defined by SEBI, are those ranked 251st onwards by market capitalisation.
claims.note: SEBI circular SEBI/HO/IMD/DF3/CIR/P/2017/114 dated October 6, 2017, defines small-cap companies as those ranked 251st onwards by full market capitalization. AMFI publishes this list.

claims.claim: This classification is updated periodically by AMFI based on average market capitalisation over a six-month period.
claims.note: AMFI updates the list twice a year (January and July) using six-month average full market capitalization data as on the end of June and December.

claims.claim: A market correction is a short-term decline in the price of a market index, bond, or commodity, typically by 10% or more from its recent peak. Corrections are considered a normal part of market cycles and are distinct from bear markets, which are more severe and prolonged declines of 20% or more.
claims.note: Multiple financial sources define a market correction as a decline of 10% or more, and a bear market as a decline of 20% or more.

claims.claim: Yes, Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) can invest in Indian small-cap stocks, either directly through a PIS (Portfolio Investment Scheme) account or indirectly through mutual funds. They must comply with FEMA regulations and RBI guidelines.
claims.note: NRIs can invest in Indian stocks through the Portfolio Investment Scheme (PIS) under FEMA regulations and RBI guidelines. This requires an NRE/NRO account, a PIS permission letter, and a Demat and trading account.

article_title: Small-Cap Corrections Narrow Post-COVID: What It Means For You
